source: Armstrong, Denniston, Gordon (1975) The use of the decomposition principle in making judgments
finding: Subjects estimated odd quantities (Polaroid film packs, tobacco, dropouts, contest cards) directly or through a given multiplicative breakdown. Decomposed groups were almost always more accurate.
numbers: 151 subjects, three groups, 13 comparisons of median accuracy ratio (larger/smaller of estimate and truth). Decomposed worse on 1 of 13, significantly better on 9 of 13 (median test, p<.05). Tobacco: 64% of direct estimates off by factor 10 or more vs 20% of decomposed. Example: Group 2 Contest direct 831.3 vs decomposed 147.8; Group 1 Film direct 21.1 vs 2.1.
limits: Student classes, quantities with large unknown magnitude, breakdown supplied by the authors. A reward had no visible effect. A printed typo (66.5 billion for 66.5 million) shows even the authors mishandle big numbers.
agent_relevance: The founding result. It is for estimating big unknown quantities, not for probabilities of events.

source: Armstrong, Denniston, Gordon (1975) The use of the decomposition principle in making judgments
finding: Benefit of decomposition was largest where the subject knew least. Ranking of problems by prior confidence matched ranking of gains.
numbers: Spearman rank agreement significant at .05 for Groups 2 and 3; Group 1 too small to test. Gains ranged from none (Dropouts, 3.1 vs 3.1 style ties) to hundreds-fold (Contest, 831.3 vs 147.8).
limits: Uncertainty was rated by the same subjects, with only 4 to 5 problems per group, so the rank test is weak.
agent_relevance: Gate O3 by how little the agent knows about the target. Do not run it on every question.
quote: The value of the decomposition principle is greatest where uncertainty is high.

source: Armstrong, Denniston, Gordon (1975) The use of the decomposition principle in making judgments
finding: Exploratory check: letting subjects decompose a problem themselves was worse than being given a decomposition.
numbers: 11 self-decomposers vs 11 given-decomposition subjects, two problems. Self-decomposition poorer on each, differences not significant.
limits: Tiny sample (n=11 per cell), not significant. Authors flag it as exploratory.
agent_relevance: The quality of the split matters. A weak self-made split may lose the gain, so check the split.

source: MacGregor, Armstrong (1994) Judgmental decomposition: when does it work?
finding: Reanalysis of two earlier studies: decomposition helped only for extreme and uncertain targets, and did nothing for the rest.
numbers: MacGregor et al. 1988 (45 subjects, 16 problems): 6 extreme/high-disagreement problems median error ratio global 99.3 vs decomposed 3.0 (reduction 96.3); 5 non-extreme low-uncertainty problems global 1.8 vs decomposed 2.3 (50% worse). Armstrong 1975, 3 extreme problems: 18.0 vs 5.7. Over the nine extreme problems the reduction was 68.3 (weighted); over six others no overall effect. Digits in the answer correlated +0.75 with interquartile range of error ratios.
limits: Post hoc split of old data. 'Extreme' defined by digit count (7 or more), an arbitrary cut. Median ratios are dominated by a few huge errors.
agent_relevance: Sharpest boundary for O3: it fixes hard-to-grasp magnitudes. On easy targets it can hurt.

source: MacGregor, Armstrong (1994) Judgmental decomposition: when does it work?
finding: New randomized experiment confirmed it. Decomposition cut error about 20-fold on extreme problems and made estimates worse on non-extreme ones.
numbers: 280 subjects, 1078 estimates, 10 problems, random assignment global vs decomposed. Extreme (3.5 million to 4.2 billion): decomposition better on 5 of 6; median error reduction 19.78x; Auto accidents 93.33 vs 1.86, Bushels of wheat 45.71 vs 6.92, Area of US 33.88 vs 1.70, TV Guide circulation 7.76 vs 10.96 (worse, ns). Not extreme (4 digits or fewer): worse on 3 of 4; median error up 458% (p<.05, two-tailed). Argentine immigrants 4.89 vs 46.77; Bank failures 10.45 vs 19.50.
limits: Volunteers from a newspaper ad. Decomposition subjects got half the problems. Some components held extreme values too (US population), and people missed that by factor 1.4 to 2. Tests on logs of ratios; combined z overstates independence.
agent_relevance: The most direct replication, with a failure. Harm on easy items is large, so the agent should test whether the parts are easier than the whole.
quote: Decomposition improved accuracy when the problem involved the estimation of extreme and uncertain values. Otherwise, decomposition often produced less accurate predictions.

source: MacGregor, Armstrong (1994) Judgmental decomposition: when does it work?
finding: Decomposition works only if the parts are easier than the target and part errors are not positively correlated. Compounding errors can explode.
numbers: Paper example: two parts each 20% high multiply to 44% error (1.2 x 1.2). Parts easier than the target for only 3 of 6 problems measured (50-cent coin, US presidents, wheat). Argentine immigrants: decomposed spread 2.14 vs global 1.00 in log10 units, no gain. Wheat met all conditions and gained.
limits: Only 6 problems had part-level spreads measured.
agent_relevance: O3 needs a check that sub-answers have lower error than the whole and that errors are independent. Otherwise multiplying amplifies bias.

source: MacGregor, Armstrong (1994) Judgmental decomposition: when does it work?
finding: Decomposition cut overconfidence a little but also lowered stated confidence. The calibration gain was modest.
numbers: Probability that estimate is within 10% of truth, 10 problems: global expected 38.9%, actual 10.9% (28.0 points over); decomposed expected 32.6%, actual 9.0% (23.6 points over). Self-rated knowledge lower under decomposition on all six rated problems (US presidents 6.16 vs 5.46). Three confidence measures correlated above .99 across six problems.
limits: Accuracy within 10% was about 10% in both groups, so both were far off even when decomposed.
agent_relevance: Decomposed estimates still need calibration; decomposition alone does not fix overconfidence.

source: MacGregor, Armstrong (1994) Judgmental decomposition: when does it work?
finding: The authors give a decision procedure for when to decompose and cite other support from the literature.
numbers: Procedure: rate uncertainty; if above midpoint, pretest with 20 subjects; if upper-quartile geometric mean has 7 or more digits, compare interquartile ranges of target, components and recomposition; use the narrower. Cited as consistent: Hora et al. 1993 (targets with 8+ digits better decomposed); Henrion, Fischer, Mullin 1993 (subjects found components easier); MacGregor and Lichtenstein 1991 (people reconcile two methods by averaging).
limits: Second-hand citations from this paper; the three originals were not opened.
agent_relevance: Cheap rule: when two ways to compute disagree, average them, and use their spread as an uncertainty signal.

source: Kalyan, Kumar, Chandrasekaran, Sabharwal, Clark (2021) How much coffee was consumed during EMNLP 2019? Fermi problems
finding: Fermi problems (estimates needing a creative breakdown) were built as a benchmark. Fine-tuned T5 did poorly when it had to find the decomposition itself.
numbers: REALFP and SYNTHFP datasets; real test split about 60% of the real set. Full setting: about 80% of generated programs run without error, yet decompositions are 'seldom meaningful' and partial credit is 'a lucky coincidence'. Programs were mostly one operation, while about 20% of problems need more. Best answer score came from writing a program and executing it, not from guessing the number.
limits: T5 fine-tuned, 2021, not a modern LLM. Table cells garbled in my text extraction, so no per-cell score is quoted. Gold programs are one of many valid ones.
agent_relevance: Writing the arithmetic as executable code beat guessing the number. Finding the right split was the hard part and the failure point.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: The retrieval forecasting system asks the model to split a question into sub-questions to drive search queries. The whole system nears the crowd, but decomposition is not isolated.
numbers: Test set after model cutoffs. System Brier .179 vs human crowd .149, accuracy .715 vs .770; unskilled 0.5 forecast = .25. Where the crowd was unsure (.3 to .7) system Brier .199 vs crowd .246. Base GPT-4-1106 Brier .208 in the baseline.
limits: Sub-questions feed search, not a Fermi combine step. No ablation that removes decomposition alone was found in the text I read. Crowd still better by .03.
agent_relevance: Decomposition for evidence coverage is cheap and part of a working pipeline; its separate value is unmeasured.

source: Radhakrishnan et al. (2023) Question decomposition improves the faithfulness of model-generated reasoning
finding: Splitting a question into sub-questions answered in separate contexts (factored decomposition) kept most of the accuracy and gave more faithful reasoning than chain of thought.
numbers: Mean accuracy over four QA tasks: zero-shot 72.8, few-shot 79.7, CoT 86.0, CoT-decomposition 85.6, factored decomposition about 81.8 (read from figure). HotpotQA: base 77.0, factored 83.0, CoT-decomp 86.7, CoT 87.3. Ordering CoT > CoT-decomp > factored > few-shot > zero-shot. Factored best on faithfulness metrics.
limits: Anthropic models of 2023, four QA tasks. Faithfulness metrics are indirect (answer changes under perturbation). Accuracy cost of about 4 points for factored.
agent_relevance: Separate-context decomposition trades a little accuracy for steps that really drive the answer. Good for audit.
quote: Decomposition-based methods achieve strong performance on question-answering tasks, sometimes approaching that of CoT while improving the faithfulness

source: Press et al. (2022) Measuring and narrowing the compositionality gap in language models
finding: Models answer the sub-questions but fail to compose them. The gap stays near 40% as models grow. Explicit sub-question asking (self-ask) narrows it.
numbers: GPT-3 family compositionality gap roughly 38-42% across sizes (does not shrink); later estimates in the paper: 42.9% ChatGPT, 23.0% GPT-4. In one set the model got 1.2% of compositional questions right while answering 80% of the sub-questions. Compositional Celebrities, InstructGPT-Davinci-002 / Davinci: self-ask 79.6% / 54.2% vs 'think step by step' 45.7% / 1.1%.
limits: 2-hop factual questions, not numeric estimates or probabilities. GPT-4 shows a smaller gap. Gap is defined only on questions where the model knows both facts.
agent_relevance: Supports O3 for composing knowledge: ask sub-questions out loud, then combine. Scale alone did not fix it.

source: Schoenegger, Jones, Tetlock, Mellers (2025) Prompt engineering large language models forecasting capabilities
finding: Large preregistered prompt test on forecasting (Tetlock and Mellers are authors): Fermi and decomposition prompts did not help Brier score. Base-rate prompts helped a little.
numbers: Study 1: 38 prompts, 100 ForecastBench questions resolving December 2024, 4 models (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3.5 Haiku, GPT-4o, Llama 3.1 405B), about 3,700 forecasts per model. Mean Brier per model .208 to .227. Mixed-model difference from control (positive = worse): Fermi Estimate +.008, Event Decomposition +.007, Time Decomposition -.008, all adjusted p=.774. Simple t-tests: Event Decomposition +.002 (p=.751), Fermi +.004 (p=.643), Time Decomposition -.013 (p=.096, adjusted .210).
limits: One-shot prompts on 2024 models, 100 questions, mixed sources. A one-line 'decompose' instruction is not a multi-step pipeline. Only Bayesian Reasoning (+.030, adjusted p<.001, worse) and Propose-Evaluate-Select were reliably harmful.
agent_relevance: Direct test of 'decompose in the prompt' on forecasting: no gain. Do not expect O3 as a prompt phrase to help probabilities. Test any decomposition on our own Brier log.
quote: Small prompt modifications rarely boost forecasting accuracy beyond a minimal baseline.

source: Schoenegger, Jones, Tetlock, Mellers (2025) Prompt engineering large language models forecasting capabilities
finding: Same study: step-by-step and reference-class prompts gave small borderline gains. Explicit Bayesian updating hurt.
numbers: Simple t-tests (difference from control, negative = better): Frequency-Based Reasoning -.019 (p=.001, adjusted .022, n=370), Base Rate First -.016 (adjusted .036), Step-Back -.015 (adjusted .036), Chain of Thought -.016 (adjusted .086). Mixed model: Bayesian Reasoning +.030, z=5.436, p<.001. Study 2 added compound prompts and o1, o1-mini; Base Rate First + Chain of Thought -.007 (ns).
limits: Gains vanish in the preregistered mixed model (adjusted p .774 for all but Bayesian). Gains are about .01 Brier on a base near .21, roughly 5%.
agent_relevance: Ceiling for single-prompt tricks: about .01 Brier or nothing. Decomposition must be shown on its own log.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-most prompting enables complex reasoning in large language models
finding: Least-to-most prompting (split into easier sub-problems solved in order) generalizes to problems harder than the examples.
numbers: SCAN length split: 99.7% accuracy with least-to-most. Last-letter concatenation, list length 12: chain of thought 37.4% with 4 independent exemplars and 38.4% with 8; the paper reports least-to-most higher (value not read in my extract). Authors checked that extra exemplars alone did not close the gap.
limits: Symbolic tasks with clean sub-problem structure, code-davinci-002 era models. Not forecasting.
agent_relevance: Easy-to-hard splitting works when the structure is clean; transfer to judgment depends on a clean split.

source: Khot et al. (2023) Decomposed prompting: a modular approach for solving complex tasks
finding: Decomposed prompting (separate prompts per sub-task, with tools) beat chain of thought and least-to-most, and let the retrieval step use a real search API.
numbers: Beats CoT and least-to-most on list reversal with longer lists and new delimiters, k-th letter concatenation, and multi-hop open-domain QA (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue) with an ElasticSearch handler. On two math QA datasets (GSM8K, MultiArith) post-processing CoT gave a 14-17 point gain. Test sets of 100 examples per variant.
limits: Small test sets. Gains rely on hand-built decompositions and per-task prompts. The math gain came from fixing formatting, not new reasoning.
agent_relevance: A swap-in structure: each sub-step can use a tool or checker. Matches O3 plus tool calls.
quote: Separate prompts are more effective at teaching hard sub-tasks than a single CoT prompt.

source: Chang, Chen, Mellers, Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment (as recorded in 04_outside_view evidence_b b01)
finding: Forecaster training that bundled comparison classes with other steps gave about 10-12% Brier gain. No arm isolates decomposition.
numbers: Year 2: trained n=205 -0.10 vs control n=194 +0.05 standardized Brier, 12% improvement (from the earlier file, not reopened).
limits: Bundled training. Decomposition effect not separated. Read from the prior file, not reopened this session.
agent_relevance: Evidence for a separate Fermi effect on real forecasting is missing; treat O3 as unproven there.
